Homeless

By: Nicola De Chaud | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
Vaya the movie is inspired by untold stories of Johannesburg. It began 8 years ago, with the Homeless Writers Project, where filmmaker Robbie Thorpe agreed to work with a group of homeless people to create opportunities for their stories to be told. Robbie set up a weekly space for homeless people to share their experiences, to reframe them and write them down. It was here that the film script for Vaya was crafted in workshops, and based on the stories of David, Madoda, Tshaba and Anthony.

David came to Johannesburg in the 90’s and joined homeless talk to eke out a living. He and Robbie initiated the Homeless writers project. He lives with friends or shares a room to keep a roof over his head.

Madoda ran away from Giyani when he was 20 to find work in Johannesburg. Impeccably turned out, one would never imagine that he often sleeps at Park Station. He runs a soccer website out of McDonalds.

Tsaba lived on the streets of Durban since the age of 12. In 2001 he came to Johannesburg on the promise of work from relatives, where he experienced betrayal and tough times. He runs a theatre group for street children.

Anthony grew up in Soweto, and got involved with drugs and gangsterism as an adolescent. During that time he did hot have a permanent home. He cleaned himself up and in 2014 moved into an RDP house with his mother. He creates posters and business cards and runs a vinyl night each Monday in Braamfontien.

We spend time with these four, exploring their histories and learning something of their traumatic and colourful lives on the streets. We visit their places of sleep, their working spaces and spend time with them at the Homeless Writers Project. The evolution of Vaya, and the true stories that make up the movie drive the narrative.

Press Release:


Homeless in Johannesburg
Madoda ran away from his home in Giyani when he was 20; Anthony has been nursing a drug
problem since he was teenager and Tsaba moved to the city to find work. They all have one thing
in common - they’ve been homeless on the streets of Johannesburg for years and now their
2
stories have inspired a movie that’s changed their lives. Carte Blanche meets these extraordinary
storytellers

Script:


Vaya script


VO/LINK: Joburg, has always been a magnate for people from across South Africa. It attracts a tide of migrants moving from rural areas to the big city...
Link: All of them searching for gold - chasing after a better life.

Madoda: Johannesburg for me was an opportunity because these things on TV you think you gonna make it when you come here.

David: The reason why I was here was simple. My dream has always been to be involved in films.

Tshaba: When you back home in the rurals, when they talk about JHB ... we grow up in a world where they say JHB is a place where things happen it’s where dreams come true.

VO: The reality is that over half a million people are unemployed in the city and many have given up looking for work. Men like Madoda Ntuli, Tshabalira Lebakeng and David Majoka often find themselves marooned.

Link: They are among the numberless thousands living rough in the city.

VO: David came to Johannesburg from Uitenhage in the late 90’s, hoping to make it in the world of film

David: I was expecting something different, expecting a world of milk and honey, but it was just the opposite.

VO: David struggled to find work and a decent place to live and for years he’s eked out a living as a freelance writer for the magazine homeless talk.

David: So when I in homeless talk, get some stipends

VO: David was often not able to find the money to pay for the roof over his head.

David: yeah there were many times, many times. If it comes to a push, you have to move to your friend.

VO: for now, David lives in a one bedroomed flat in Hillbrow, which he shares with 20 other adults. He lives from month to month and could be out on the streets anyday.

VO: Madoda Ntuli often chooses the streets over a crowded room.

Madoda: You always in danger, cause if you sleep you dunno whats doing to happen

VO: Seven years ago, he unexpectedly found himself homeless. He was locked out of his room in a run down building in Jeppe with nothing but the clothes on his back. A stranger to the city, Madoda had no where to go.

Madoda: After that there is no-one to talk to. You are shattered. So I had to move, go to park station because I would have seen people sleeping there.

VO: Park station became Madoda’s home. It cost him R10 to keep his clothes in a locker and R10 to have a shower. For years he kept this secret,

Madoda: You know when you live on the streets you feel shame and you want to protect yourself and you don’t know the reaction what people will say if you say you live there....

VO: Proud and proper, Madoda makes sure he’s turned out in clean suits each day. Men like Madoda and David challenge the stereotype of a homeless person as criminal - someone who is dirty, lazy or bad.

David: people don’t understand homelessness, they just think that they chose to be there
Some people they have situations that are beyond their control.

VO: Despite his situation, Madoda hussles for business everyday. He hangs out at Mcdonalds, where he runs a soccer website and posts press releases and updates daily.

Madoda: Ja it’s a double life in a way, I hide it, I couldn’t tell anyone and even myself I wouldn’t feel it. The only time comes back that I’m homeless is around 4 when everybody is going home and me I’m not going home

VO: In his make-do space, David continues to write for homeless talk and some years ago contributed to a book which was made into a TV Series called ‘A place called home’.

Robbie: Homelessness is really for me about vulnerability, Its the vulnerability of not having a fixed abode.

LINK: In 2008 film maker Robbie Thorpe was confronted outside his offices by an angry young man demanding to know what had happened to the writing royalites for the TV series ‘A place called Home’.

Robbie: And he was one of the writers on the book and he said you’ve stolen from me

David: I was on a fact finding mission

LINK: The facts were, that the SABC owned the rights, and that neither David, nor Robbie had any claim to royalties.

Robbie: I felt sorry for the guy, and I sort of I think to appease him, I said, well look, why don’t we try and do something else

David: He said I can organize some guys, who were interested to come through and tell their stories and come through and take it from there..

Robbie: He arrived with a group on Thursday and they sort of never left.

VO: The group met once a week for 8 years to put aside the grind of everyday and simply tell stories.

Robbie: So it was a space in which people were trying to tell the more dramatic things that had happened in their lives, and often those dramatic things are secrets and things they have never told anybody

Anthony: Not even my family knows about this story that I’m sharing you know.

VO: The group grew and shrunk over the years and eventually the core of four including Anthony Mafela remained to drive the project.

LINK
After 8 years of telling and listening, the group began to craft a script for a movie based on their life stories

Robbie: I always knew I would have to find a vehicle that was a multi story vehicle ... and the idea of people coming to town on a train together just became the device. They themselves had come to town.

Tshaba: Hey friends, I’m going to Joburg baby! I’ll be back rich!

Upsound:movie

Robbie: Very early on they talked about the invisibility of being homeless and how people don’t see you. If they did a story it was to make them visible....

VO: No one character was one person, but each was imbued with different facets of stories that had been told. Madoda told of how he was robbed as a new guy on the streets.

Madoda: When I started sleeping, I wake up without my shoes, so that night, I dont know maybe I was tired. They left their old one.

VO:Anthony told of how he was caught in a world of drugs and gangsterism

VO: The film was directed by Akin Omotoso

Akin: Whatever you do don’t water down the story

VO: The four were integral to the making of the film - The managed the translations worked on set and scouted locations in an around Johannesburg with Akin
